Though the new reign had made him free to return to the capitals, he continued to live in the country, remarking that anyone who wanted to see him could make the hundred-mile trip from Moscow to Bald Hills, while he himself needed nobody and nothing. He liked to say there are only two sources of human vice—idleness and superstition—and only two virtues—activity and intelligence. He personally oversaw his daughter's education, and to develop these two virtues in her, gave her lessons in algebra and geometry until she was twenty and organized her life so that every hour was accounted for. He himself was perpetually busy: writing his memoirs, solving problems in higher mathematics, turning snuffboxes on a lathe, working in the garden, or supervising the construction that was always underway on his estate. Since regularity is the first condition of productivity, regularity in his household was maintained to the highest degree of precision. He always came to meals not just at the same hour but at the same minute. With everyone around him, from his daughter down to the servants, the prince was sharp and unfailingly demanding—not out of cruelty, but with a severity that inspired the kind of fear and respect that few genuinely cruel men could have commanded. Although he was retired and no longer wielded political influence, every senior official appointed to the province felt duty-bound to pay him a visit, and they waited in his lofty antechamber—alongside the architect, the gardener, and Princess Mary—until the prince appeared at precisely the appointed time.
